docs.title: re-back User Guide
docs.text:
re-back is a backup agent for Linux that stores files in a Backblaze Computer Backup account. It speaks the same protocol as the Backblaze desktop client, so the Backblaze website sees the machine and its files as a normal computer backup — but the agent runs on your Linux machine, NAS, container host, or Kubernetes cluster.

Independent project. re-back is not made by or affiliated with Backblaze. It is an independent implementation of the client protocol. Use it with an account and data you control, and test a restore before relying on it.

This guide is for the person installing and running re-back. You do not need to know how the protocol works, but you should be comfortable with a terminal, editing a configuration page in a browser, and mounting the folders you want to protect.

docs.title: What re-back does
docs.text:
• Connects a Linux machine to your Backblaze Computer Backup account.
  • Backs up one or more local folders, presenting each one to Backblaze as a Windows drive letter (C:, D:, and so on).
  • Runs a first full backup, then incremental backups. Files that have not changed are not uploaded again.
  • Can run continuously in the background, or only when you press Start.
  • Can restore files from this machine or from another machine on the same Backblaze account.
  • Optionally encrypts the backup with a private backup key that only you hold.

docs.title: The four screens
docs.text:
The web interface has four sections:

Screen What it is for Home Overall status, machine account creation, and machine renaming Backup Start, pause, resume, and stop a backup; view recent runs Backup settings Global defaults, include/exclude rules, backup key, and source volumes Restore Sign in, choose a source machine, select files, and restore them

docs.title: Before you install
docs.text:
You will need:

  • A Backblaze account with Computer Backup available.
  • A Linux machine that can reach Backblaze over HTTPS.
  • Enough local disk for re-back's own state. This is much smaller than the backed-up data, but it grows with the number of files. A few gigabytes is usually plenty for a personal library; very large file counts need more.
  • Permission to read every file you want to back up. Running the service as root is the simplest way to avoid silently skipping protected files.
  • A decision about where the web interface can be reached. It has no login for the settings and backup controls, so keep it on localhost, a private network, or behind a VPN. Do not expose it directly to the internet.

docs.title: Recommended first run
docs.text:
1. Install re-back.
  2. Open the web interface and create the machine account.
  3. Set a backup key if you want private encryption.
  4. Add at least one source volume.
  5. Run a backup and confirm it completes.
  6. Restore a test file to a temporary folder. Do this before you depend on the backup.

docs.title: Words used in this guide
docs.text: Term Meaning Machine account The entry for this installation in your Backblaze account. Backblaze calls these computers. Volume One local folder tree that re-back backs up. Each volume is shown to Backblaze as a drive letter. Drive letter The letter Backblaze uses in file paths, such as D:. It is a label, not a real Windows drive. Backup key An optional private encryption passphrase. When one is set, nobody — including Backblaze — can read the backup without it. State re-back's local records: identity, file index, run history, and restore history. Losing some of it can force a full re-upload. Restore in place Put files back at their original paths on this machine. Only allowed for this machine's own backup.

docs.title: A note on safety
docs.text:
re-back is early software. Keep a second copy of anything irreplaceable until you have completed a restore test and are confident in the setup. The Restore screen is the source of truth for whether a backup is usable; a green backup status alone is not proof.

Next: Install re-back.

docs.title: How a backup runs
docs.text: Backups are automatic once the machine account and volumes are configured. There is no per-file selection during a normal run: re-back compares the source volumes with its local index and uploads what is new or changed.

docs.title: Starting a backup
docs.text:
1. Open Backup.
  2. Click Start.

The buttons on that screen are:

Button What it does Start Begins a backup run now. Pause Stops starting new work while leaving the run in place. Resume Continues a paused run. Stop Ends the current run. Completed work is kept; the next run continues from the index. Settings Opens Backup settings.

If the daemon is enabled, re-back also starts backups on its own schedule. The daemon does not start runs while Paused is ticked, but a manual Start still works.

docs.title: The first backup
docs.text:
The first run has to read and upload everything that matches your volumes and filters. It is the slowest run.

During the first run re-back:

  1. Walks each configured source volume.
  2. Applies the global and per-volume include/exclude rules.
  3. Reads file metadata and content fingerprints.
  4. Uploads file data to Backblaze.
  5. Records what completed in its local index.

Large libraries can take hours or days depending on file count, file sizes, disk speed, and upload bandwidth. This is normal. You can leave it running, and you can stop and resume later without starting over.

docs.title: Later backups
docs.text:
Later runs are incremental:

  • A file whose size and modification time have not changed is normally skipped.
  • A new or changed file is read, fingerprinted, and uploaded.
  • If two files have identical content, re-back can reuse the stored copy instead of uploading the same bytes twice.
  • A file that has disappeared from a volume is recorded as deleted, so the backup follows the source over time.

Deleted-file handling is the reason for the mount-marker option. If a network mount vanishes, re-back must not conclude that every file was deleted. Use Require .bzre_mounted for NFS/SMB volumes; see Backup settings.

docs.title: What happens on the wire
docs.text:
At a high level:

  1. re-back authenticates as the machine account. Routine backups do not need your Backblaze password.
  2. It asks Backblaze where to upload.
  3. It uploads file data in chunks, in parallel, and checks the result.
  4. It records the completed files locally and finalizes the run's file list with the server.
  5. The local index and run history are updated so the next run knows what is already protected.

You do not need to manage any of these steps. The Backup screen shows progress, counts, speed, and any error reported by the server.

docs.title: Status and logs
docs.text:
The Home and Backup screens show:

  • whether a run is active,
  • how many files and bytes are done,
  • current speed and estimated time,
  • the last error, if any.

Run history and per-file results are kept in the state directory. On a systemd install, service logs are available with:

sudo journalctl -u re-back -f

In Docker:

docker compose logs -f

docs.title: Stopping, pausing, and interruptions
docs.text:
• Pause is for a short break. The run stays in place.
  • Stop ends the run. Files already completed stay completed.
  • A crash, reboot, or lost connection does not invalidate the backup. Start again and re-back continues from its index.
  • If the same file was partially uploaded, the next run verifies the completed chunks and fetches only what is missing.

Do not delete the state directory, the index, or the volume's Volume ID to "fix" a slow or stuck backup. That can force a full re-upload and make the server treat the volume as new.

docs.title: What re-back does not do
docs.text:
• It does not create a Backblaze account or change your Backblaze plan.
  • It does not decide how long Backblaze keeps old versions. That is controlled by your Backblaze account settings.
  • It does not mount a network share for you. Mount it with the operating system before re-back starts.
  • It does not back up a volume whose source path is missing. Fix the mount or path first.

docs.title: A safe routine
docs.text:
1. Let the first backup finish.
  2. Change one test file.
  3. Run another backup and confirm the change is recorded.
  4. Restore that file to a temporary folder.
  5. Only then treat the backup as tested.

Next: Restore files.

docs.title: Backup settings
docs.text:
Open Backup settings from the left navigation, or the Settings button on the Backup screen.

The page has two parts:

  • Global — settings that apply to every volume.
  • Volumes — one card per source folder, with its own path, drive letter, and optional filters.

Changes are not live until you click Save configuration at the bottom of the page. Saving affects the next scan. A backup that is already running keeps the settings it started with.

docs.title: Transfer and schedule
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Upload threads 4 Number of files uploaded in parallel. Range 1–64. More threads can improve throughput but use more memory and bandwidth. Rescan every (minutes) 60 How often the background daemon looks for changes. A rescan is a stat-only walk and is normally cheap. Scan load threshold 0.7 Pauses scanning briefly when the system load is above this fraction of CPU capacity. A negative value disables load backoff. Change debounce (seconds) 5 Waits this long after a file change before rescanning, so a burst of writes becomes one scan. Paused Off Stops the daemon from starting automatic backups. A manual Start still runs. Useful during maintenance. Enable scan daemon Off Runs incremental backups forever on the rescan interval. This is the always-on mode. Manual backups work whether it is on or off. Watch local volumes for changes (fsnotify) Off Triggers an earlier rescan when a local file changes. It has no effect on NFS or SMB; the periodic rescan still catches those changes.

Which mode should I use?

  • Manual: leave the daemon off and press Start on the Backup screen when you want a run. Good for a laptop or an occasional backup.
  • Always on: enable the daemon. It rescans on the interval and uploads changes without you pressing anything.
  • Maintenance: tick Paused to stop automatic runs without disabling the daemon.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text: Filters decide which files are eligible. They apply during the scan; they do not delete anything already backed up until a later scan records the file as gone.

docs.title: Pattern syntax
docs.text:
All patterns are case-insensitive. There is no regular-expression mode.

Pattern Meaning *.jpg Any file whose name ends in .jpg, at any depth Photos/* Everything below Photos at the volume root; * also crosses / *backup* Any path containing backup file?.txt file1.txt, fileA.txt, but not file10.txt node_modules Any path containing node_modules (plain text is a substring) */.cache/* Any .cache directory and its contents, at any depth

Rules that are easy to get wrong:

  • A pattern without / is matched against the file name at any depth. So *.tmp works everywhere.
  • A pattern with / starts at the volume root. Photos/* does not match a folder called Old/Photos unless you write *Photos/* or a full path.
  • The full local source path also works, for example /mnt/media/Photos/*.
  • * matches any run of characters including /. ? matches exactly one character.
  • Plain text with no * or ? is a substring match, not an exact match.
  • Excludes always win over includes.

docs.title: Global include patterns
docs.text:
One pattern per line.

  • Empty means every file is eligible.
  • If a volume has its own include list, that list replaces the global list for that volume. It does not add to it.

docs.title: Global exclude patterns
docs.text:
One pattern per line.

  • These apply to every volume.
  • A volume's own exclude list is added to this list.
  • Use this for things you never want to upload: temporary files, caches, build output, and similar.

Examples:

node_modules
*.tmp
*/.cache/*
/var/lib/docker/*

docs.title: Apply native mandatory excludes
docs.text:
This checkbox is on by default. It applies Backblaze's own mandatory exclusion list, which is the list the native desktop client always honors. It keeps re-back from uploading files Backblaze considers unsuitable, such as operating-system internals and temporary files.

  • The list is read from the state directory at bzdata/bzexcluderules_mandatory.xml.
  • It is re-read on every scan. If you replace that file with a newer copy from a Backblaze release, the new rules apply on the next scan without rebuilding re-back.
  • Turning it off lets you back up files that the native client would skip. This is usually a bad idea.
  • Turning it off does not remove files that are already in the index. They stay indexed and may be uploaded on the next backup.

docs.title: Client identity
docs.text:
These fields control how re-back identifies itself to Backblaze. Most people should leave them alone.

Field Meaning Running build The actual re-back program version. This is not the Backblaze version. Configured spoof The Backblaze client version re-back reports on the wire and in its User-Agent. Server advertises The latest Windows client version Backblaze publishes for this cluster. Client version Editable version string, such as 10.0.3.1075. It must look like a dotted version.

Buttons:

  • Refresh advertised asks Backblaze for its current published version.
  • Adopt latest copies the advertised version into Client version.
  • Save configuration applies the change.

Changing the reported version does not change the re-back build. If a backup starts failing after a Backblaze client update, refresh the advertised version, adopt it, save, and try again.

docs.title: Backup key
docs.text:
The backup key is an optional private encryption passphrase for this machine's backup.

  • If you set one, the data is encrypted with a key derived from your passphrase. Backblaze cannot read it without the passphrase.
  • Store a copy somewhere safe before you continue. If you lose the passphrase, the backup cannot be restored. There is no recovery reset.
  • Set the key before the first backup if you plan to use one.
  • A generated 50-character key is available in the interface. Save it in a password manager or another safe place, not only in a browser tab.
  • If this machine's backup already has a key, the page shows Rotate instead of first-time setup. Rotation requires the current passphrase.
  • Remove key un-gates future backups. It does not decrypt or re-encrypt data that is already stored; older data remains protected by the old key. Keep the old passphrase if you may need to restore that data.

If you are restoring a machine that has a private key, the Restore screen asks for the key. See Restore.

docs.title: Volumes
docs.text:
Each volume is one local folder tree. Backblaze sees it as a Windows drive letter.

First install: the built-in default is one volume at /backups on drive C:. That is a placeholder. Change the path to a real folder, or remove it and add your own, before the first backup. A volume whose path does not exist cannot be backed up.

docs.title: Adding a volume
docs.text:
1. Click + Add volume.
  2. Enter the Source path — an absolute path on the machine or container, such as /mnt/photos.
  3. Choose a Drive letter that is not used by another volume.
  4. Optionally set include and exclude patterns for this volume.
  5. Optionally enable Require .bzre_mounted at this volume root.
  6. Click Save configuration.

The volume's Volume ID is created when you save. Keep it. It is how the server recognizes the same volume across restarts.

docs.title: Volume fields
docs.text: Field Notes Source path The local directory to back up. It must exist when a backup starts. Missing paths are not silently invented. Drive letter The letter Backblaze sees, such as D:. Each volume needs a unique letter. Changing it changes how paths appear in the backup, so set it once. Include for this volume If non-empty, this list replaces the global include list for this volume. Empty means inherit the global list. Exclude for this volume Extra excludes added to the global list. Empty means only the global excludes apply. Require .bzre_mounted Skip this volume unless a file named .bzre_mounted exists at its root. Use it for NFS/SMB mounts. Volume ID Server-side identity, minted on first save. Do not remove and re-add a volume casually.

docs.title: Why the mount marker matters
docs.text:
A network mount can disappear while the machine is still running. Without a guard, every file on that volume looks deleted, and the backup could record a mass deletion.

If you enable Require .bzre_mounted:

  1. Create an empty file named .bzre_mounted at the root of the mounted filesystem.
  2. Enable the checkbox for that volume and save.
  3. re-back skips the volume whenever the marker is missing.

When the mount comes back, the marker is visible again and the volume is processed normally.

docs.title: Changing a volume later
docs.text:
• Changing the source path is allowed, but think of it as pointing the same server-side volume at a different local tree.
  • Changing the drive letter changes the paths Backblaze records. Avoid it after the first successful backup.
  • Removing a volume does not delete its backup immediately, but the server will eventually see the files as gone. If you want to keep them, leave the volume configured.
  • Adding a second volume with the same drive letter is rejected. Use a unique letter for each.

docs.title: Volumes inherited from another machine
docs.text: An inheritance brings the source machine's volumes across with their drive letters and volume IDs already set, and with an empty path: the last step of the wizard asks where each drive lives on this machine. Nothing is walked until you answer that. A drive you leave blank keeps its identity and its backed-up files but is not scanned here.

docs.title: Clearing backup state
docs.text:
At the bottom of the page, under Dangerous, Clear backup state resets this machine's backup state. Type CLEAR BACKUP to confirm.

It removes the identity, the ledger of what has been sent, the scan index, the account and host binding, the inherit record, and the encryption settings — including the passphrase and the key that wraps your file keys. The daemon stops.

It keeps the volume list (paths, drive letters, volume IDs), the include/exclude rules, the schedule, the run history and the logs, so re-creating the machine does not mean re-typing them.

It does not delete backed-up data from the account. Files already uploaded stay there; only this machine's record of them is gone. Encrypted files whose passphrase was discarded may no longer be readable.

Next: How a backup runs.

docs.title: Report a problem
docs.text:
Support is handled directly by the maintainer — use the contact you were given with your release.

Before you report:

  1. Check Troubleshooting.
  2. Reproduce the problem once and note the exact steps.
  3. Include the re-back version shown in the interface and your install method.

Useful details:

  • What you expected to happen.
  • What actually happened.
  • The exact error message.
  • Whether the problem affects backup, restore, or the web interface.
  • A short log excerpt from the service or container.

Redact before posting: account email addresses, passwords, 2FA codes, backup keys, machine IDs, and private file paths.

docs.title: Read the documentation
docs.text:
This guide is the end-user documentation for re-back, published at https://rebackoss-org.github.io/re-back-user-guide/. The source lives in a private repository, so it is not linked from here.

Separate protocol and file-format notes exist for people who want to understand the client protocol, native file formats, and internal backup mechanics. They are not published; none of it is needed for normal use.

docs.title: Learn the backup model
docs.text:
If you are unsure where to start:

  1. Install re-back
  2. Create the machine account
  3. Configure backup settings
  4. Understand the backup process
  5. Restore a test file

docs.title: Feature requests
docs.text:
Open an issue with the label or prefix feature request and describe:

  • the problem you are trying to solve,
  • what you would like the interface or behavior to do,
  • whether it affects one machine or many.

For moving an existing backup onto new hardware (or onto another OS), see the inheritance workflow.

docs.title: Inheritance workflow
docs.text:
Inheritance adopts a machine that is already backing up to your account. The new install takes over that machine's identity, its ledger of what has been sent, and its drive list — so the server sees a machine it already knows, and only new or changed files get uploaded. Nothing is re-uploaded and nothing already on the account is moved or deleted.

Use it when you are retiring the machine that used to back up: another PC, a Windows box you are moving off, a reinstall of the same host.

docs.title: What inheritance is for
docs.text:
• Move a backup to new hardware. The new machine keeps the old machine's file history instead of starting a second, duplicate set of files.
  • Move a backup to another OS. A Windows install's C: and D: drives can be presented from a Linux box without the server noticing the difference.
  • Recover from a broken install. If the local state is lost but the account still has the machine, inheritance pulls the state back down.

docs.title: What comes across
docs.text:
Inheritance moves the record of the backup, not the files:

item carried notes machine identity (host GUID, account binding) yes the account keeps seeing one machine, not two ledger of every file already sent yes seeded into the local index, so nothing is re-uploaded drive list and volume IDs yes the folders holding those drives are chosen in step 3 server-side file numbering yes new files continue above the inherited counter the backed-up files themselves no they stay on the account; use Restore to get them back the source's encryption key or passphrase no if the source used private encryption, keep that key — restores still need it your exclude rules, schedule and other local settings no this install's own settings are left alone

The source machine is retired on the account when the transfer commits: it shows up renamed old_inactive_… and marked as divorced. Do not start its client again — inheritance pauses this install, but the server is never told anything, so a source that kept running would still be pushing under the same backup.

It is not a restore. Inheritance brings across the record of what is backed up; restoring brings back the files themselves. If you want files back, use Restore.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Sign in with your account password. Inheritance asks the server for your machine list, and that call needs the password — a session that was restored from a saved key cannot do it. Sign in on the machine card first.
  • The target machine must have no backup identity yet. If it already backs up, the button is greyed out with a ? next to it: clear the current backup state first (see Clearing backup state).
  • The source machine must still be listed on the account. Inheritance reads the source's state archive from the server. Machines that cannot be inherited are shown greyed out in the picker with the reason.
  • Quit the source's backup client first. It is retired on the account once the transfer commits, and nothing here can pause it remotely.
  • Have the folders ready. The last step asks where each of the source's drives lives on this machine. You can also skip a drive and map it later.

Inheritance pauses backups. It does that locally — the daemon is not started and nothing is sent — so the old and new machine can never both push. The server is not told anything about being paused.

docs.title: 1. Pick the machine to inherit from
docs.text:
On Home, in the machine account card, press Inherit existing backup. Choose the source machine from the dropdown and press OK.

The source's name is not reused: a throwaway host is registered for the transfer (tmp-inhrt-…), and the server retires it once the state has been committed. If the transfer fails before that point, the throwaway host is kept so you can retry without starting over.

docs.title: 2. Wait for the transfer
docs.text:
The wizard shows the download, the commit and the adoption as they happen: archive size, ledger file and line counts, then the index seeding. Backups stay off for the whole step.

If it fails, backups stay off and the error is shown with the server's reason. Press OK again to retry — a retry after the commit never re-commits the archive, so a half-finished transfer cannot double-apply.

docs.title: 3. Map the source's drives to folders here
docs.text:
The state archive knows the source's drives (C:, D:, …) but not where those drives live on this machine, so this is the last step and it cannot be asked earlier. Each drive is listed with the number of files the inherited ledger has for it; type the folder that drive's root is mounted at.

The drive letter is the identity. A file at /mnt/nas/movies/a.mkv on this machine, with D: mapped to /mnt/nas, is still presented to the server as:

D:\movies\a.mkv

That is byte-for-byte the path the old machine used, so the server recognises the file instead of uploading a copy. Ledger paths are never rewritten — only the root folder is local. Both of these are the same mapping:

This machine D: mapped to Presented as /mnt/nas/movies/a.mkv /mnt/nas D:\movies\a.mkv /mnt/win-d/movies/a.mkv /mnt/win-d D:\movies\a.mkv

Rules the wizard enforces:

  • One folder per drive, never nested. A file belongs to the first root that contains it, so D: inside C:'s folder would file one drive's data under the other's identity. Overlapping roots are refused.
  • The folder must exist and be readable. A path that is not there now would fail the first backup anyway.
  • Blank means skip. A drive you leave empty keeps its identity and its backed-up files, but nothing under it is walked here. Its files stay on the account; a restore of those files will ask you for a destination.
  • At least one drive has to be mapped. Skipping all of them would finish the inherit with nothing to back up, so it is refused — clear the backup state instead if you meant to abandon it.
  • One folder per drive letter, and not a folder this machine already backs up: two roots over the same files would present them twice.

Press Save mapping. The gate clears, the daemon starts and the index is rebuilt from the inherited ledger against the folders you chose.

docs.title: Verifying the result
docs.text:
• Home shows the source machine's identity, not a new one, and the backup state is no longer paused.
  • Backup → status reports a file check that is clean rather than frozen, and the file and byte totals match what the account already had.
  • Run one backup. It should send nothing (or only what changed since the source last ran) — if it starts uploading the whole corpus, the drive mapping is wrong: the paths it is producing do not match the ledger.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The button is greyed out. Hover the ? beside it. Either you are not signed in with a password, or this machine already has an identity — clear the backup state first.

It stopped at "waiting for a local folder". The identity and ledger are adopted; only the drive mapping is left. Reloading the page returns to the mapping pane. It is also reachable headlessly: GET /api/v1/inherit/status lists the pending drives (each with its letter, file count and volume ID), and POST /api/v1/inherit/map takes one decision per drive — a folder, or "skip": true:

{
  "volumes": [
    { "vol_guid": "v000…123", "path": "/mnt/win-d" },
    { "vol_guid": "v000…456", "skip": true }
  ]
}

Every pending drive needs a decision (incomplete_mapping otherwise), and a rejected mapping applies nothing. A successful call clears the gate and starts the daemon, exactly as Save mapping does. Like every other step that changes state, inherit/map needs this app's session cookie (inherit/status does not), so sign in first or send the same session the web UI uses.

It failed before finishing. Backups stay off and the throwaway host is kept. Press OK to retry. If the retry cannot proceed, clear the backup state and start again.

A mapped drive says its folder is not readable. Fix permissions on the host, then re-enter the path. Nothing was applied — a mapping is all or nothing.

The first backup wants to upload everything. The mapped root does not correspond to the drive's real contents, so the relative paths do not line up. Remove the mapping and point the drive at the folder that actually holds its tree.

Backups stay frozen after a successful inherit. The account holds an older, larger copy of a file-check manifest than the inherited ledger rebuilds. The client declares the shrink to the server instead of re-uploading; if a run still reports bzcf_shrunk_on_client, update the client and re-run.

You added a file on a day the source already backed up. Nothing to do. A manifest the account already holds may not be re-sent smaller, and ours rebuilds denser than the other client's, so the client re-encodes that day's manifest with weaker compression until it clears the held size — logged as bzcomb grow <date>: rebuild … re-encoded … — and uploads it. The records are unchanged; only the compressed bytes differ. A day with no new files is still only declared, never uploaded.

docs.title: Clearing backup state
docs.text:
Backup settings → Dangerous → Clear backup state resets this machine: the identity, the ledger, the scan index, the account and host binding, the inherit record, and the encryption settings — including the passphrase and the key that wraps your file keys. The daemon stops. Type CLEAR BACKUP to confirm.

It keeps what describes what to back up: the volume list with its paths, drive letters and volume IDs, the include/exclude rules, the schedule, the run history and the logs.

It does not delete backed-up data. Files already on the account stay there and belong to the account, not to this install. Encrypted files whose passphrase you just discarded may no longer be readable, though, so clear only when you mean it.

This is also the way out of an inheritance that is stuck: clearing removes the adopted identity so a fresh inherit (or a fresh machine) can start.

Next: Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Create the machine account
docs.text:
A machine account is this installation's identity in your Backblaze account. Backblaze uses it to group the backup, count the computer against your plan, and show the machine in the restore picker.

You create it once. Routine backups do not need your Backblaze password again.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
• Have your Backblaze account email and password ready. If the account uses two-factor authentication (2FA), have the current code ready.
  • Decide on a machine name. This is the name you will see in Backblaze and in re-back's restore screen.
  • Do not create a second machine account for an installation that already has one. Reinstalling over a kept state directory will reuse the existing identity.

re-back does not create a Backblaze account. It attaches this machine to an account you already have.

docs.title: Create the account
docs.text:
1. Open the web interface. The first screen is Login, with a Machine account card.
  2. Enter the Backblaze account email and password.
  3. If the account uses 2FA, tick My account uses 2FA and enter the current code.
  4. Click Sign in.
  5. Enter a Machine name, then click Create machine account.

On success, re-back stores the machine identity in its state directory and the card shows the machine as linked. Your password and 2FA code are used for this request and are not saved by re-back.

docs.title: Choosing a machine name
docs.text:
Use a name that tells you what the machine is and where it lives:

  • Good: media-server, office-nas, basement-backup
  • Less useful: linux, server2, test

The name is a label, not a hostname requirement. It does not have to match the Linux hostname. It can contain spaces, but a short name without spaces is easier to read in a list. The interface accepts up to 120 characters.

If you leave the name blank, re-back generates a timestamped name such as re-back-20261112_093000. That works, but it is harder to recognize later.

docs.title: Renaming later
docs.text:
The Machine account card has a Rename action. Renaming changes the display name only. It does not change the backup's file paths, the machine's identity, or the data already stored.

If the server cannot confirm the rename immediately, re-back keeps the local name and retries the server update on a later sync. The card will tell you whether the server confirmed it.

docs.title: If account creation fails
docs.text:
Check, in this order:

  1. Email, password, and 2FA code. Use the current code; codes expire quickly.
  2. Network access. The machine needs HTTPS access to Backblaze.
  3. Account state. Confirm the account is active and has Computer Backup available.
  4. Existing identity. If the state directory already contains an identity, do not mint another one. Check the Machine account card first.

Do not repeatedly create machine accounts to work around a login failure. Each successful creation adds another computer to your Backblaze account.

docs.title: Protect the identity
docs.text:
The machine identity is stored in the state directory. It is as sensitive as a password: it lets this installation act as this machine. Keep the state directory private (0700 is appropriate), and do not copy it to another machine unless you are deliberately moving the installation.

A normal restore does not require copying the identity. If this machine is lost, install re-back elsewhere, create a new machine account, sign in on the Restore screen, and select the old machine as the restore source.

Next: Configure backup settings.

docs.title: Install re-back
docs.text:
re-back is a single executable. There is nothing else to install beside it — the files it needs on first start are built into the binary. Choose the method that matches where you want it to run:

  • Linux install script (systemd)
  • Native binary without the script
  • Docker Compose
  • Kubernetes

All options need a Backblaze account and outbound HTTPS access. The web interface listens on port 8080 by default.

Keep the web interface private. Settings and backup controls are not password-protected. Anyone who can reach the port can change what is backed up, start a backup, or start a restore. Use localhost, a private LAN, a firewall, or a VPN. Do not publish port 8080 on the internet.

docs.title: Option 1: Linux install script (recommended)
docs.text: The script installs a systemd service, keeps configuration separate from the large state directory, and starts re-back at boot.

docs.title: 1. Get a binary
docs.text:
re-back is distributed to invited users; there is no public download page. Use the re-back binary from the release you were given and put it at deploy/re-back.

Building from source requires access to the private repository. With Go 1.27 or newer, from a source checkout you already have access to:

(cd app && go build -trimpath -ldflags "-s -w" -o ../deploy/re-back .)

docs.title: 2. Run the installer
docs.text:
sudo bash deploy/install.sh install --bin "$PWD/deploy/re-back"

The installer places:

What Where Program /usr/local/bin/re-back systemd unit /etc/systemd/system/re-back.service Configuration /etc/re-back/config.json State (identity, index, run history) /var/lib/re-back Logs /var/log/re-back

By default the service runs as root, because a backup agent that cannot read a protected home directory silently misses files. To run with less privilege:

sudo bash deploy/install.sh install --bin "$PWD/deploy/re-back" --user re-back

The re-back user must be able to read every source volume. A system user with no home directory will not be able to read another user's 0700 home folder unless you grant access deliberately. Check before choosing this option.

docs.title: 3. Open the interface
docs.text:
On the same machine:

http://localhost:8080

From another machine on your private network, use the server's address:

http://SERVER-IP:8080

If the page does not load, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: 4. Service commands
docs.text:
sudo systemctl status re-back
sudo systemctl restart re-back
sudo journalctl -u re-back -f

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
Build or copy the new binary over deploy/re-back, then run the installer again. It replaces the program and unit but leaves configuration and state in place:

sudo bash deploy/install.sh install --bin "$PWD/deploy/re-back"

docs.title: Remove
docs.text:
sudo bash deploy/install.sh uninstall

This removes the program and service but keeps all backup state, so a later install can pick up where it left off.

sudo bash deploy/install.sh purge

This also deletes configuration, identity, indexes, and restore history. The next install will need a new machine account. Do not use purge as a normal upgrade step.

docs.title: Option 2: Native binary
docs.text: Use this when you want to run the binary yourself, for example under your own service manager, in a one-off test, or inside a system you already manage.

docs.title: 1. Build
docs.text:
Building requires access to the private repository. With Go 1.27 or newer, from a source checkout you already have access to:

(cd app && go build -trimpath -ldflags "-s -w" -o ../re-back .)

If you received a prebuilt binary, use that and skip this step.

docs.title: 2. Create its directories
docs.text:
sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/re-back /var/log/re-back
sudo install -d -m 0700 /var/lib/re-back

docs.title: 3. Run it
docs.text:
Run as root so it can read everything you select:

sudo env \
  BBAPP_CONFIG_DIR=/etc/re-back \
  BBAPP_STATE_DIR=/var/lib/re-back \
  BBRE_API_LOG=/var/log/re-back/api-wire.log \
  BBAPP_ADDR=:8080 \
  ./re-back

BBAPP_ADDR=:8080 listens on all interfaces. To restrict access to the local machine, use BBAPP_ADDR=127.0.0.1:8080.

If you do not set BBAPP_CONFIG_DIR and BBAPP_STATE_DIR, both default to /config. That is useful in a container, but usually wrong for a host install.

For a permanent service, use the unit file in deploy/re-back.service as a starting point, or use Option 1 and let the installer manage it.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Variable Default Purpose BBAPP_ADDR :8080 Web interface listen address BBAPP_CONFIG_DIR /config Directory containing config.json BBAPP_STATE_DIR value of BBAPP_CONFIG_DIR Identity, indexes, run history, and other mutable state BBRE_API_LOG unset Optional wire log for troubleshooting; may contain sensitive request data, so protect it

For a normal host install, set config and state to separate directories. This keeps the large, changing state out of /etc.

docs.title: Option 3: Docker Compose
docs.text: The Compose file builds or pulls the image, publishes port 8080, and keeps configuration and state in named volumes.

docs.title: 1. Edit the source mounts
docs.text:
Open docker-compose.yml and add a read-only mount for each folder you want to protect:

    volumes:
      - re-back-config:/config
      - re-back-data:/data
      - /mnt/photos:/mnt/photos:ro
      - /mnt/documents:/mnt/documents:ro

The paths on the right are inside the container. Use those container paths when you add volumes in the web interface.

docs.title: 2. Start it
docs.text:
docker compose up -d --build

If you want to use the published image instead of building locally, comment out the build: line first.

docs.title: 3. Open the interface
docs.text:
http://localhost:8080

To keep the port off other network interfaces, change the port mapping to:

    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"

docs.title: 4. Logs and storage
docs.text:
docker compose logs -f

re-back-config holds config.json. re-back-data holds the identity, index, and run history. Do not remove these volumes unless you intend to start over.

The container runs as root by default so it can read mounted source trees. If you switch to a non-root user, make sure the UID can read every mount.

docs.title: Option 4: Kubernetes
docs.text: The manifest in deploy/k8s.yaml creates a single-replica Deployment, a Service, and a 50 GiB ReadWriteOnce volume for configuration and state.

docs.title: 1. Review the manifest
docs.text:
• Increase the PVC size if you have a very large file count.
  • Pin the image tag instead of using latest if you need reproducible upgrades.
  • Add a volume and volume mount for each source tree you want to back up.

The template does not include any source mounts. Without one, re-back has nothing to back up.

Example addition to the Deployment:

          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
            - name: photos
              mountPath: /mnt/photos
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: re-back-data
        - name: photos
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: re-back-source-photos

Create the source PVC, or use another volume type appropriate for your cluster. Then use /mnt/photos as the volume path in the web interface.

docs.title: 2. Apply it
docs.text: kubectl apply -f deploy/k8s.yaml

docs.title: 3. Reach the interface
docs.text:
The manifest does not create an Ingress. Use a port-forward for the initial setup:

kubectl port-forward deploy/re-back 8080:8080

Then open http://localhost:8080. For permanent access, put it behind your normal private ingress or VPN. Do not expose it publicly without adding authentication.

docs.title: 4. Important limits
docs.text:
• Keep one replica. The state volume is ReadWriteOnce and the agent is designed as a single instance.
  • Do not delete the PVC to "restart" the pod. That deletes the machine identity and the file index.
  • The container needs enough CPU, memory, and temporary disk while hashing and uploading. The manifest's requests and limits are a baseline, not a guarantee.

docs.title: After installation
docs.text:
Open the web interface. On first start re-back creates the files it needs under its state directory. You should see the Login screen with an empty Machine account card.

Next: Create the machine account.

docs.title: Restore files
docs.text:
Restore is a separate operation from backup. You choose files from a machine's backup, choose where they should land, and start a download.

Restoring does not change the backup in the cloud. It only reads from it.

docs.title: Restore needs a sign-in
docs.text:
The Restore screen uses an authenticated Backblaze session. If you are not already signed in — for example after a restart — it asks for your account email and password, plus a 2FA code if the account uses 2FA. This is required even when restoring this machine's own backup, because the screen must list the machines on the account and fetch their file lists.

  • The sign-in is for this restore session. Your password is not saved by re-back.
  • If the service restarts or the session expires, sign in again.
  • Routine backups do not need this sign-in; they use the machine identity.

docs.title: Restore from this machine or another machine
docs.text:
1. Open Restore.
  2. Sign in.
  3. Under Restore from machine, choose the source:
  4. this machine, or
  5. another machine on the same Backblaze account. If you create a new machine account while already signed in, click Refresh next to Load to re-fetch the list without reloading the page or signing in again.
  6. Click Load. re-back fetches that machine's file list.
  7. If the machine's backup is marked with a lock (🔒), provide its backup key as described below.
  8. Select files and folders.
  9. Choose the destination and options.
  10. Click Download selected.

The file picker is a tree. Checking a folder selects everything under it. Select all and None are shortcuts; Re-scan refreshes the list from the server.

docs.title: Private-key backups
docs.text:
If the source machine's backup was created with a backup key, the restore cannot read it without that key.

  • Use saved key uses a key already available to this installation. It only works if it is the same key that protects that machine's backup.
  • Enter own key lets you type the passphrase for this restore session. The typed key is not saved.
  • This screen can use a saved key, but it cannot change or remove the key. Key management is on Backup settings.

If the key is wrong, the restore cannot decrypt the data. There is no override and no recovery reset. Use the passphrase you escrowed when the key was set.

docs.title: Choose where the files go
docs.text: There are two modes.

docs.title: Restore to another folder
docs.text:
This is the safe default and the only mode allowed when restoring another machine's backup.

  1. Enter a Destination folder.
  2. Leave Restore in place unchecked.
  3. Click Download selected.

re-back writes the files under the destination using their original folder structure, with the Windows drive letter removed. For example:

C:\Users\alex\Photos\cat.jpg

is restored as:

DESTINATION/Users/alex/Photos/cat.jpg

The destination must:

  • be writable by the user running re-back,
  • have enough free space for the selected files,
  • be a path visible inside the container or pod when using Docker or Kubernetes.

If you restore into an existing folder, files at the same relative paths can be overwritten. Use a new or empty folder when you are unsure.

docs.title: Restore in place
docs.text:
Restore in place puts each file back at its original local path.

It is available only when the restore source is this machine's own backup. re-back refuses in-place restore from another machine because that machine's drive mappings would point at the wrong places on this host.

In-place restore:

  • recreates missing parent folders,
  • opens each target file and prepares it for the expected size,
  • downloads the missing or damaged chunks,
  • can overwrite files at those paths.

Treat it as a repair operation, not a merge. If you are testing a restore, use a temporary destination instead so you do not overwrite live data.

docs.title: Force full download
docs.text:
Force full download (overwrite everything) is available for in-place restore. It skips the verify-and-skip pass and downloads every chunk again.

Use it when:

  • the local disk is failing and existing reads cannot be trusted,
  • a previous in-place restore produced files that still look wrong.

Without it, re-back verifies existing chunks and skips the ones that are already correct, which is faster and usually what you want.

docs.title: Parallel jobs
docs.text:
Parallel jobs controls how many files are downloaded at once, from 1 to 20. The default is 4.

Higher values can be faster until Backblaze starts answering with a busy or retry response. re-back backs off and retries automatically, but a very high number can make the restore slower. Raise it gradually.

docs.title: While it runs
docs.text:
The Restore status card shows progress, file counts, bytes, speed, and any error.

  • You can leave the page; the restore continues in the background.
  • Reloading the page does not cancel the run.
  • Starting a second restore while one is running returns "a restore is already running".
  • If a run fails, Retry — resume in place appears. It retries the same selection and destination, skipping chunks that already verify.

Do not start a second restore to the same destination while the first is still running.

docs.title: After the restore
docs.text:
1. Open a few restored files, including one large file and one from a deep folder.
  2. Compare them with the originals or with a known-good copy.
  3. Only then rely on the backup.

If files are missing from the picker, check the source machine and the backup date; the picker shows what the server has for that machine. If files restore but are unreadable, stop and check the backup key and the restore status before overwriting anything else.

docs.title: Restore quick reference
docs.text:
Goal Mode Get a copy without touching live files Destination folder, Restore in place off Repair this machine's files at their original paths Restore in place on, this machine as source Recover from a failing local disk Restore in place + Force full download Recover files from an old or replaced machine Destination folder; in-place is not allowed Test that the backup is usable Destination folder, then open the restored files

Next: Inheritance workflow (placeholder).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Start with the service status and the current screen. Most problems are one of: the web interface is not reachable, the machine account is missing, a source path is not readable, or a restore is waiting for a key.

docs.title: The web interface does not load
docs.text:
Check that re-back is running:

# systemd install
sudo systemctl status re-back

# Docker
docker compose ps
docker compose logs --tail=100

# Kubernetes
kubectl get pods
kubectl logs deploy/re-back --tail=100

Then check:

  • Port: the default is 8080.
  • Address: BBAPP_ADDR=:8080 listens on all interfaces; BBAPP_ADDR=127.0.0.1:8080 listens only on localhost.
  • Firewall: allow the port only from the network you trust.
  • Docker port mapping: 8080:8080 publishes it; 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 keeps it local.
  • Kubernetes: the manifest has no Ingress. Use kubectl port-forward deploy/re-back 8080:8080.

If the service is running but the page is blank, reload once and check the browser console. If it still fails, include the service log in a bug report.

docs.title: Sign-in or machine account creation fails
docs.text:
• Confirm the email and password by signing in at Backblaze directly.
  • For 2FA, use the current code; codes expire quickly.
  • Confirm the machine can reach Backblaze over HTTPS.
  • If the account already has a machine for this installation, do not create another one. Check the Machine account card first.
  • If the account is new, confirm Computer Backup is available on it.

Repeated failed sign-ins can be rate-limited by Backblaze. Wait before trying again.

docs.title: Backup will not start
docs.text:
Check these in order:

  1. Machine account exists. The Home screen should show a linked machine. If not, complete initial setup.
  2. At least one volume exists and its source path exists. A missing mount or a typo in the path means there is nothing to scan.
  3. The service user can read the source. On a systemd install the default is root. If you chose --user re-back, test with sudo -u re-back ls -la /path/to/source.
  4. Another run is already active. The status card will say so. Wait for it to finish or stop it.
  5. Paused is not the same as stopped. Paused blocks only automatic daemon runs; Start should still work.
  6. The daemon is off. That is fine for manual backups; press Start.

Read the error line on the Backup screen. It usually names the failing path or the server response.

docs.title: The first backup is taking a very long time
docs.text:
The first run reads and uploads the whole selection. That is expected.

Things that help:

  • Let it run; stopping and starting does not lose completed work.
  • Raise Upload threads gradually if the machine and network have headroom.
  • Check the Scan load threshold; a low value can slow scanning on a busy machine.
  • Check free space for re-back's state; a full state disk stops progress.
  • Check the upload bandwidth outside re-back.

Do not delete the index or state to make it faster. That forces a full re-upload and can make the server treat the volume as new.

docs.title: Files are missing from the backup
docs.text:
Check, in order:

  1. Global include list. Empty means everything; a non-empty list limits the selection.
  2. Volume include list. If present, it replaces the global include list for that volume.
  3. Excludes. Excludes always win. A pattern like *.tmp or a plain substring can match more than you intended.
  4. Native mandatory excludes. This is on by default and skips files the native Backblaze client skips. Turn it off only if you deliberately want those files.
  5. Permissions. A file the service cannot read is skipped. This is common with 0700 home directories when running as a non-root user.
  6. Mount marker. If Require .bzre_mounted is on and the marker is missing, the whole volume is skipped.
  7. The file is on a different volume than the one you configured.

After changing filters, save the configuration and run another backup. Filters apply on the next scan, not to a run already in progress.

docs.title: A network volume vanished and the backup looks like it deleted everything
docs.text:
Stop the backup first.

  1. Check that the NFS/SMB mount is actually present.
  2. Remount it at the same path.
  3. Confirm the files are visible from the host.
  4. For the future, enable Require .bzre_mounted on that volume and create the marker file at the mount root.

Do not delete the machine account or the state directory to "reset" this. That can turn a temporary mount problem into a permanent identity problem. If the server has already recorded deletions, contact the project with the run details before taking destructive action.

docs.title: Restore will not start
docs.text: Message or symptom Check Asked to sign in Restore always needs an account sign-in, even for this machine No machines in the list Confirm the account and that the machine has completed a backup "a restore is already running" Wait for the current restore or let it finish; only one runs at a time Locked machine Enter the backup key for that machine Key rejected Use the exact passphrase; there is no recovery reset Destination error Use a writable path with enough free space Docker/Kubernetes restore writes nowhere useful The destination must be a mounted path visible inside the container or pod

docs.title: Restore finished but files are wrong or unreadable
docs.text:
• If the backup uses a key, confirm you used the correct one.
  • Check the restore status for skipped files, partial files, or warnings.
  • Try restoring to a different empty folder rather than in place.
  • For a failing local disk, use Restore in place with Force full download so existing bad chunks are not trusted.
  • Keep the failed output until you have a good restore; do not overwrite it.

docs.title: The backup key is lost
docs.text:
There is no recovery reset. The data encrypted with that key cannot be restored without it. Search your password manager and any escrow copy you made when the key was created.

If you still have access to the machine and its saved key, export or record the key before changing anything. Do not remove the key from the account hoping to make old data readable; removal affects future backups, not existing encrypted data.

docs.title: Docker or Kubernetes sees the wrong paths
docs.text:
The source path in re-back is the path inside the container or pod, not the host path.

  • Docker: if you mount /mnt/photos on the host to /mnt/photos in the container, configure /mnt/photos.
  • Docker: if the host path is different, use the container side of the mount.
  • Kubernetes: add a volume and volume mount to the Deployment, then use that mount path.

The same rule applies to restore destinations. A destination that is not mounted will be written inside the container's temporary filesystem and may disappear when the container is replaced.

docs.title: Where the files live
docs.text:
Install method Configuration State and logs Install script / systemd /etc/re-back/config.json /var/lib/re-back, /var/log/re-back Native binary BBAPP_CONFIG_DIR BBAPP_STATE_DIR, BBRE_API_LOG Docker /config in the container /data in the container Kubernetes /data/config in the pod /data/state in the pod

State includes the machine identity, file index, backup history, and restore history. Treat it as sensitive and do not delete it during ordinary troubleshooting.

docs.title: Before opening an issue
docs.text:
Include:

  • the re-back version shown in the interface,
  • the install method (systemd, binary, Docker, Kubernetes),
  • what you expected and what happened,
  • the exact error text,
  • a short, redacted log excerpt.

Remove account emails, passwords, 2FA codes, backup keys, machine IDs, and any private file paths before posting.

Next: Get help.
